affected_parts.quote: Symptoms on leaves, known as Glomerella Leaf Spot (GLS), express as brown angular spots ... The fungi may also overwinter in twigs, buds, and fruit scars

summary.value: On fruit, symptoms appear as flat to sunken necrotic lesions (0.5 to 6 cm), light to dark brown, progressing toward the core in a V-shaped pattern; lesions begin as small, slightly sunken circular spots that may be surrounded by a red halo on mature fruit and can develop concentric rings with pink or orange spore masses. On leaves, Glomerella Leaf Spot appears as brown angular spots that may merge into irregular blotches.
summary.quote: symptoms often manifest as flat to sunken necrotic lesions on fruit ... the lesions typically range from 0.5 to 6 cm. They are light to dark brown and progress to the core of the fruit in a V-shaped pattern ... Symptoms on leaves, known as Glomerella Leaf Spot (GLS), express as brown angular spots sometimes merging and forming irregular blotches.

diagnostic_features.value: After making a cross-section of the infected fruit a V-shaped, brown, watery lesion that extends toward the core can be observed, distinguishing it from other summer fruit rots (white rot and black rot).
diagnostic_features.quote: After making a cross-section of the infected fruit a V-shaped, brown watery lesion can be observed (Figure 3). This is a key diagnostic feature of bitter rot, which distinguishes it from other summer fruit rots (i.e. white rot and black rot).

value: Integrate good sanitation, cultural practices, and chemical control
Prune trees to remove and destroy dead or diseased wood, including shoots infected with fire blight, and burn it to reduce inoculum
Chopping/flail-mowing dead wood on the ground to remove bark and increase decomposition
Remove and burn (eliminate) mummified fruit from trees and the orchard floor throughout the growing season
Maintain tree vigor with a balanced fertility program (based on soil/foliar analyses), proper watering, and annual pruning
Do not use susceptible cultivars; select resistant cultivars and prune canopies open and well-ventilated to reduce surface wetness
Apply fungicides from fruit set / first cover until harvest where a good sanitation program is in place

Rotate FRAC groups to reduce fungicide-resistance risk (FRAC M multisite: captan, ziram, ferbam; FRAC 7 benzovindiflupyr; FRAC 11 pyraclostrobin/trifloxystrobin/picoxystrobin; FRAC 29 fluazinam; FRAC 12 fludioxonil postharvest)
Use drip/under-canopy irrigation to prevent spore dispersal by water splash
Select a good planting site (plant on hilltops instead of valleys)
Biological control: Serenade ASO (Bacillus subtilis QST713), DoubleNickel55 (B. amyloliquefaciens D747), Theia (B. subtilis AFS032321), Howler (Pseudomonas chlororaphis AFS009)
Consult the New England Tree Fruit Management Guide for current fungicide recommendations
treatments.quote: Growers are encouraged to rotate FRAC groups to alleviate the risk of fungicide resistance development. ... irrigating under the canopy with drip irrigation prevents spore dispersal by water splash. Initial infections can be reduced through resistant cultivar selection and canopy pruning. ... Removal of mummified fruit and diseased twigs from the tree canopies and their destruction is an important step ... pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Pear Scab is a fungal disease caused by Venturia pirina pathogen

type_of_disease.quote: Pear Scab is a fungal disease caused by Venturia pirina pathogen

value: Foliar
Stem
Fruit
affected_parts.quote: that can affect the leaves, shoots, and fruit of pear trees

summary.value: Pear scab first appears as small yellow or chlorotic spots, often on the undersides of leaves, with larger more obvious patches on fruit; lesions start as olive-colored circular spots that turn dark brown or black and become soft, and infected fruit often cracks open.
summary.quote: Pear scab often appears first on undersides of leaves as small yellow, or chlorotic spots. It can be hard to notice on leaves. On fruit, these same patches appear larger and are more obvious. Given time, infections will turn black and soft.

diagnostic_features.value: All lesions start as olive-colored circular spots that transition to dark brown as the infection progresses; on leaves lesions are more visible on the bottom of the leaf, shoot lesions are usually easily visible (and can be walled-off or sloughed off), and infected fruit often cracks open from the skin lesions.
diagnostic_features.quote: All lesions start as olive-colored circular spots that transition to dark brown as the infection progresses. Shoot lesions are usually easily visible. They can be walled-off or sloughed off the shoots. On leaves the lesions are more visible on the bottom of the leaf, but overall can be hard to identify.

value: apple scab
look_alikes.quote: Like apple scab (V. inaequalis), pear scab creates lesions on leaves and fruit which impact overall tree health and fruit production.

value: Break up leaf and branch residues from previous seasons (mowing or other mechanical means) to reduce inoculum
Apply urea or other nitrogen-based fertilizer to leaves in late fall to break down leaves more quickly and reduce inoculum
Apply lime prior to leaf fall to reduce overwintering inoculum
Plant pear varieties with reduced susceptibility (Barnett Perry, Batjarka, Brandy, Erabasma)
Apply protective fungicides ahead of estimated rain events between delayed green tip and petal fall (Propiconazole, Myclobutanil, Tebuconazole)
Organic options: copper octanoate (copper soap), sulfur, Bordeaux mixtures, mineral oil or neem oil
Do not apply copper and Bordeaux after bloom (russeting risk); apply only between green tip and full bloom
treatments.quote: Breaking up residues like leaves and branches from previous growing seasons, by using a mower or other  mechanical means, reduces the amount of inoculum present. ... Fungicides are the most commonly available and economically effective method to manage pear scab. ... Propiconazole, Myclobutanil, Tebuconazole. ... Organic options are available, such as copper octanoate (copper soap), sulfur, Bordeaux mixtures, and mineral oil or neem oil. ... Copper and Bordeaux should not be applied after bloom, as russeting, may occur.
